channel.title: Action Global News
channel.description: Independent news on AI, business, markets, small business and global ecommerce.

item.title: Israel's president gives Gadi Eisenkot, not Benjamin Netanyahu, the first chance to form a government
item.description: Eisenkot won more recommendations than Netanyahu, but his own bloc is well short of a majority. He is calling for a national emergency government, and Netanyahu stays prime minister until a new one is sworn in.

item.title: China's factory-gate prices rose 5.7% in October, the fastest pace in more than four years, while consumer inflation slowed to 0.7%
item.description: Mining and raw materials are pushing up what Chinese factories charge, but households are seeing little inflation. The split points to strong outside demand and a weak home market.

item.title: Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset
item.description: Nvidia's directors say they have no reason to think company or national security secrets leaked, but they will review the reports anyway. Huang, who told staff he had an affair with the woman at the center of the reports, says he will stay on as CEO.

item.title: Jeffco Public Schools' two tax measures are trailing, and a recount on 5A looks likely as the district plans for cuts
item.description: Voters in Jefferson County appear to have turned down two property tax measures for Jeffco Public Schools. The teacher pay measure is close enough for a recount, and district leaders say more budget cuts are coming either way.

item.title: FTC orders Delta, Uber, Walmart and six other companies to explain how personal data shapes prices and worker pay
item.description: The Federal Trade Commission has started a study of whether airlines, ride-share and delivery apps and two big retailers charge different people different prices, or pay different workers different rates, based on personal data. It is a study, not a lawsuit. Responses are due within 45 days of receipt.

item.title: Google says it will honor one shared robots.txt signal for AI training opt-outs, but not until 2027
item.description: Google announced on October 30 that it plans to support a shared, machine-readable way for websites to say no to AI training. The signal lives in robots.txt and comes from an IETF draft. It is not live yet, and today's controls, including Google-Extended, stay in place.

item.title: Two FTC cases in five days target payment-processing fees and hard-to-cancel contracts for small businesses
item.description: The Federal Trade Commission filed two actions against payment companies that sell to small businesses. One is a lawsuit against restaurant-software maker Toast that Colorado joined. The other is a settlement with a Washington processor. Both turn on the same question: what a business agrees to when it signs up, and what it costs to leave.

item.title: Airbnb's third-quarter revenue grew 19% to $4.9 billion, and the company added up to $12 billion in buybacks
item.description: The home-sharing company's bookings and profit grew in the summer quarter, according to its shareholder letter. It also guided to 16% to 18% growth for the fourth quarter and said its own AI trip-planning agent is coming in 2027.

item.title: New Zealand's election is too close to call, with National and Labour level on the party vote
item.description: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says his National Party has a path to keep governing, but Labour has not conceded. Hundreds of thousands of special votes still need counting, and the new Opportunity Party is headed into Parliament.

item.title: Lakewood police name Agent Nicholas Graham, 33, as the officer killed in a shootout on an RTD bus
item.description: A Lakewood police agent died and three others were wounded Thursday evening when a man they approached on an RTD bus opened fire. The suspect was killed when officers shot back, and an outside team is investigating.

item.title: Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production in Texas by mid-2027 to build more Cybercabs
item.description: The pickup that Tesla once expected to sell by the hundreds of thousands is being phased out. Musk says the floor space will go to the driverless Cybercab, while sales data point to weak demand.

item.title: A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison over the Shakahola starvation deaths
item.description: The sentence follows Mackenzie's October conviction for 191 murders tied to his Good News International Church. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, and his lawyer says he will appeal.

item.title: Colorado voters approved Amendment 87, replacing the 4.4% flat income tax with graduated rates starting in 2027
item.description: Colorado will return to a graduated income tax for the first time since 1986. Rates fall on the first $100,000 of income and rise on income above roughly $500,000.

item.title: U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than forecast, and unemployment slipped to 4.1%
item.description: Hiring in October came in well above what economists expected, and earlier months were revised higher. The stronger numbers add to expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise rates in December.

item.title: The $6.3 billion Binance theft is the largest crypto hack on record. How exchange hacks happen, who is behind them, and what holders and businesses can check
item.description: Each of the last three record-setting crypto thefts has been attributed by the FBI to North Korea. The pattern matters to anyone who keeps coins on an exchange, accepts crypto from customers, or holds it on a company balance sheet.

item.title: Marvell agreed to buy laser maker Lumentum for about $115 billion in stock, betting that AI data centers will move to light
item.description: The chipmaker is paying 4.5 of its shares for each Lumentum share to own the lasers and optical parts that move data inside AI data centers. Both stocks fell, and the deal is not expected to close until 2028.

item.title: Apple's revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion last quarter, closing its biggest year ever, with tariff refunds adding to the margin
item.description: iPhone and Mac drove the September quarter, while iPad and wearables shrank. Apple said refunds of tariffs it had paid added about a point to its gross margin.

item.title: Binance reopened withdrawals after a $6.3 billion theft the FBI blames on North Korea, and customers pulled out $3.6 billion on the first day
item.description: The exchange says it has bought back 90% of the stolen tokens with its own money. The rest are harder to source, and only some coins and networks were reopened at first.

item.title: It is Election Day in Colorado. Ballots must reach election officials by 7 p.m., and certified results are not due until late November
item.description: Mail is no longer a safe way to return a ballot. Drop boxes and voter service and polling centers are open until 7 p.m., and the first results posted tonight will be unofficial.

item.title: Small contractors are turning to AI voice assistants to answer leads in minutes, and federal consent rules decide how far they can go
item.description: Research going back to 2011 shows most businesses answer web inquiries slowly. A new wave of AI voice tools, including one launched this month by a Denver firm that shares ownership with Action Global News, promises a callback within a minute, but federal rules treat those voices as artificial and require the caller's consent.

item.title: Two critical PHP flaws sent governments scrambling to take websites offline. What PHP2Shell is, who is exposed, and what to do if you run a site
item.description: On October 21 the PHP project shipped fixes for two remote code execution flaws in the language that runs most of the web. Within hours, attack attempts were counted in the millions, government sites in Europe went dark as a precaution, and security agencies told anyone who could not patch to unplug. Here is what happened, in plain terms, and the checklist a small business with a WordPress or other PHP site should work through this week.

item.title: Colorado regulators are hearing Xcel's plan to make data centers pay their own way on the grid. Here is what is in it
item.description: Xcel proposes minimum bills, long contracts and collateral for new loads of 50 megawatts or more. Consumer and environmental groups say a fast-track option for confidential deals could undercut those protections.

item.title: A Denver judge rejected a last-minute bid to knock Amendment 87, Colorado's graduated income tax measure, off the ballot
item.description: The challenge argued that signatures gathered by improperly registered petition circulators should be thrown out. The judge ruled the law does not allow that remedy. Ballots are already in voters' hands.

item.title: The U.S. ordered non-emergency staff and families out of Saudi Arabia as an attack on Dammam's airport killed one person
item.description: Saudi aviation authorities said an attack on King Fahd International Airport killed one person and injured eight. It follows deadly attacks on Riyadh's main airport earlier this month.

item.title: Putin agreed in principle to resume three-way talks on Ukraine after November 10, and freed a jailed American, as strikes hit Kyiv
item.description: The Kremlin set no date, and earlier rounds this year produced little beyond prisoner exchanges. The same night, Russian strikes killed civilians in Kyiv and near Kharkiv.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment after surgery for an early lung cancer, his doctors say
item.description: Final tests confirmed a localized adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, and found no spread. His doctors say nothing medical stands in the way of a South America trip next month.

item.title: Screwworm has been found in U.S. wildlife for the first time, and in a beef cow in southern New Mexico
item.description: The flesh-eating parasite, eradicated from the United States decades ago, has been moving north through Mexico. Officials announced both detections on October 21 and are widening surveillance and fly trapping.

item.title: Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case, a traveler from Uganda, as the Bundibugyo outbreak reaches a fifth country
item.description: The patient, a woman who arrived in Abuja on an international flight from Uganda, is in isolation and 44 contacts are being traced. The outbreak that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May has now produced more than 9,600 confirmed cases.

item.title: The FAA has certified Boeing's 737 MAX 10, the largest 737, clearing the way for deliveries of more than 1,500 ordered jets
item.description: The approval completes certification of all four 737 MAX models. The plane also brings a new angle-of-attack safety system that will become standard across the family.

item.title: eBay is cutting about 9% of its staff in its second round of layoffs this year, and Comcast is reported to be planning cuts of its own
item.description: eBay's chief executive told employees the company's strategy is working and that it wants to move resources to its fastest-growing areas. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Comcast is preparing a significant number of job cuts.

item.title: United and Southwest both posted record revenue, then cut their profit outlooks because jet fuel is eating the gains
item.description: Both airlines say travelers are still booking at higher fares. The problem is the cost of flying them: fuel prices well above what the carriers planned for in the summer.

item.title: Tesla's profit fell 43% last quarter as it started building Optimus robots and promised Cybercab sales by year-end
item.description: Revenue was flat at about $28 billion and spending on research jumped. Tesla said the first production-quality Optimus humanoid robots are coming off a converted line in Fremont, California, and executives said they want Cybercabs in customers' hands before 2027.

item.title: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found it misled Facebook users about their data
item.description: The penalty, set on October 21, follows a September jury verdict that Meta made misleading statements about how much control Facebook users had over their data. The money would go to New Mexico schools. Meta says it expects to win on appeal.

item.title: Social Security checks will rise 3.6% in 2027. What the raise is worth, what else changes, and the dates to know
item.description: The Social Security Administration announced the cost-of-living adjustment on October 14, the day September inflation data came out. It is the biggest raise since 2023, and it arrives with a higher payroll tax cap and new limits for people who work while collecting.

item.title: Holiday airfares are at 10-year highs, and a federal rule starting Oct. 19 narrows what counts as the airline's fault. When to book, and what you are still owed
item.description: Jet fuel costs and fewer low-cost seats have pushed Thanksgiving and Christmas fares to their highest level in a decade. At the same time, a Department of Transportation rule taking effect October 19 changes how ten kinds of disruptions are classified, which can affect the meals and hotels airlines offer when things go wrong.

item.title: ACA open enrollment starts Nov. 1 with premiums up again and no enhanced subsidies. The deadlines, the numbers and what to check before you renew
item.description: Proposed 2027 marketplace premiums are up about 15% at the median, and the extra federal subsidies that cushioned buyers through 2025 are gone. A court fight over the enrollment calendar is still on appeal. Here is what shoppers, the self-employed and small employers should know.

item.title: Shipping small orders to Europe this holiday season now costs more. The EU's €3 parcel duty, the €2 handling fee due Nov. 1, and what sellers outside the bloc should do
item.description: Europe ended duty-free treatment for parcels worth up to €150 this summer. Two more changes are scheduled for November 1, just as holiday orders start shipping. Here is how the charges stack up on a typical order, and who actually pays them.

item.title: Apple's smart home push: HomeView, a $299 Apple TV, a new HomePod mini and its own cameras and locks. What was announced, what it costs and what to know first
item.description: At its October 13 event, Apple introduced a seven-inch home hub, a new Apple TV and HomePod mini, and a line of cameras, locks and thermostats built with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The common thread is Siri AI, which is still in beta and not available in the European Union.

item.title: Nearly one in three Denver listings cut its price in September, the second-highest share among big metros. What the record price cuts mean for buyers and sellers
item.description: Nationally, 20.8% of homes for sale had a price reduction in September, the highest share for the month in Realtor.com's records. Denver's share was 32.1%, behind only Salt Lake City. Inventory is close to pre-pandemic levels, but higher mortgage rates are limiting how many buyers can take advantage.

item.title: New SBA loan rules took effect Oct. 1. Buying a small business with a 7(a) loan now takes more cash, more proof and a citizenship check
item.description: The Small Business Administration's updated lending rulebook applies to every 7(a) and 504 loan numbered on or after October 1. The biggest changes land on people buying, expanding or buying out a business, and they are easier to plan around before a letter of intent than after.
